analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge as wilderness, barring oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Environment Committee until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law that about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the coastal plain known as the 1002 Area — are wilderness under the Wilderness Act. Wilderness designation is the strongest land protection available: it would permanently bar oil and gas drilling, road building, and most development on that land. It also would have blocked the push, active at the time, to open the refuge to oil drilling.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public that owns the refuge: the coastal plain, calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and habitat for polar bears and migratory birds, would be permanently shielded from industrial development. Future generations would keep the option of protecting it, which drilling would foreclose forever.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public that owns the refuge

how_it_helps.text: Designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's 1002 Area as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, the strictest protection federal land can carry [S3].

Wilderness designation permanently prohibits oil and gas leasing, roads, and most development, so the refuge's coastal plain could never be opened to drilling by a future Congress's budget or lease sale.
The bill had 23 cosponsors, including one Republican (Sen. Lincoln Chafee), showing organized support for permanent protection [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose any future access to one of the largest untapped onshore prospects in the country, and Alaska's government loses potential revenue from drilling leases. Consumers do not directly pay anything, though wilderness permanently forecloses a possible future source of domestic oil.

drawbacks.text: The designation would permanently lock in about 1.56 million acres of federal land against any development, foreclosing a potential domestic oil supply and the federal and state revenue that leasing could produce [S3].

Supporters of drilling have long argued the drilling footprint on the coastal plain would be small and that the area holds significant recoverable oil; wilderness designation would make that trade-off impossible to revisit, permanently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is real but narrow: foregone drilling revenue and a possible future oil supply, borne mostly by industry and Alaska. The benefit is permanent, irreversible protection of one of the country's largest intact wild areas — the kind of thing that is nearly impossible to undo once lost. The bill's only real flaw is that it never had a chance to be argued on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the bill on February 2, 2005, with 24 original senators joining him [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; the committee never held a hearing or markup, and no vote ever occurred [S5].
The bill makes wilderness designation a matter of permanent law rather than leaving the coastal plain's fate to each year's budget fights [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies seeking access to the refuge's coastal plain are better off, because wilderness designation would have permanently closed the area to drilling and the bill's death kept that door open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies seeking refuge drilling access

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the wilderness designation bill and recruited 24 colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: 23 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. James Inhofe (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Pushed to open the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to oil drilling, making wilderness protection for the same area a non-starter with Senate leadership.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 23 cosponsors were 22 Democrats and a single Republican, and the committee chaired by a Republican that buried it took no action at all.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently bar drilling on the refuge's coastal plain, foreclosing leases and revenue the industry had sought there for decades. Its interest in the bill ran directly against the public's interest in keeping the refuge undeveloped.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and drilling-linked contractors
industries.note: The state would forgo potential royalties, jobs, and pipeline revenue from coastal plain development.
